about.pitch: Meet Felipe, a Senior Software Engineer focused on building tools, pipelines, and systems for VFX, animation, and real-time content. A natural problem solver, he builds technology that removes complexity from creative workflows, giving artists and teams more time to focus on what they do best. With over five years of commercial software engineering experience and an MSc in Computer Animation and Visual Effects, he combines software engineering with hands-on experience in computer graphics, rendering, simulation, and pipeline development.

dccTranslation.title: DCC Translation Pipeline
dccTranslation.description: Maya to Unreal Engine USD translation pipeline.

media.alt: Dcc translation Unreal Engine 5 imported items
Dcc translation Unreal Engine 5 imported scene

blocks.text: A validation-driven Maya to OpenUSD pipeline for standardising scene publishing between Maya and Unreal Engine. Maya scene data is extracted into a lightweight, DCC-independent SceneGraph, validated against configurable rules, converted to USD, and published with structured metadata.
The pipeline separates each stage of the publishing process:

items.title: Scene Extraction
items.text: Maya DAG hierarchy, transforms, geometry and metadata are converted into a SceneGraph.

items.title: Validation
items.text: YAML rule profiles check the scene before publishing.

items.title: USD Export
items.text: The validated SceneGraph is translated into a structured OpenUSD stage.

items.title: Publishing
items.text: Publish metadata is generated and translation activity is recorded.

items.title: Unreal Engine
items.text: The resulting USD stage can be imported while preserving scene hierarchy and per-object separation.

blocks.text: The SceneGraph acts as the intermediate representation between Maya and OpenUSD. It stores the essential structural data required for cross-DCC translation and USD stage construction, keeping the core publishing system independent from Maya.
Scenes are validated using configurable YAML profiles covering:

items.text: Naming and hierarchy
Supported node types
Transforms and geometry
Scene scale

blocks.text: The Maya plugin provides the artist-facing validation and publishing workflow, while a CLI exposes the same functionality for command-line workflows.

Publishing generates structured metadata and records translation activity through interchangeable registry backends. SQLite supports local workflows, while MongoDB provides a database-backed option. The project also includes automated testing with Nox and mayapy and a drag-and-drop Maya installation workflow.
The completed pipeline provides a standardised path from Maya scene data to Unreal Engine through OpenUSD, with validation and publishing handled as separate stages.

items.title: Validated publishing
items.text: Invalid scenes can be identified before USD export.

items.title: DCC-independent translation
items.text: The SceneGraph separates Maya extraction from USD publishing.

items.title: Structured USD output
items.text: Scene hierarchy and per-object separation are preserved for Unreal Engine.

items.title: Tracked publishing
items.text: Publish metadata and translation activity are recorded through SQLite or MongoDB.

items.title: Multiple workflows
items.text: The system is accessible through the Maya plugin and CLI.

wavefront.title: Adaptive Wavefront Path Tracer
wavefront.description: C++17 CPU wavefront path tracer investigating adaptive scheduling for coherent rendering.

media.alt: XYZRGB Dragon Scene USD scene render

blocks.text: A CPU-based wavefront path tracer developed for an MSc research project investigating whether adaptive workload scheduling can improve execution coherence and rendering performance. The renderer uses C++17, OpenUSD and Embree, with a modular scheduling framework that allows different workload ordering strategies to be evaluated within the same rendering pipeline.

The research focuses on the shading stage, where rays can diverge across materials, textures and shader operations. The project investigates whether runtime information can be used to make better scheduling decisions than static material or texture sorting.
The renderer separates path tracing into independent stages connected by work queues:

items.title: Scene Loading
items.text: OpenUSD scenes are loaded into internal geometry, material, texture and camera representations.

items.title: Ray Generation
items.text: Primary camera rays are generated and stored in the RayQueue.

items.title: Traversal
items.text: Embree performs BVH intersection and produces shading records for rays that hit the scene.

items.title: Scheduling
items.text: The ShadingQueue can be reordered using the selected scheduling policy.

items.title: Shading
items.text: BSDF evaluation, direct lighting and secondary ray generation are performed on the reordered workload.

items.title: Iteration
items.text: Secondary rays are returned to the RayQueue and the process continues until paths terminate or reach the maximum depth.

blocks.text: The renderer uses separate RayQueue and ShadingQueue structures implemented using a Structure of Arrays layout. This separates traversal data from shading data and provides explicit points where workloads can be reorganised before execution.

items.title: RayQueue
items.text: Stores ray origins, directions, throughput, pixel coordinates and path depth.

items.title: ShadingQueue
items.text: Stores hit positions, normals, material and texture IDs, and path information required for shading.

items.title: Scheduling
items.text: Policies generate a sorted index order before the queue is materialised for shading.

blocks.text: Keeping scheduling separate from the queue implementation allows different scheduling strategies to be evaluated without changing the rest of the renderer.
The renderer implements a physically based path tracing pipeline with direct and indirect lighting, supporting diffuse, metallic, dielectric and emissive materials.

items.title: Next Event Estimation
items.text: Explicitly samples light sources to estimate direct illumination.

items.title: Multiple Importance Sampling
items.text: Combines light sampling and BSDF sampling using the power heuristic.

items.title: Adaptive Sampling
items.text: Uses Welford's online algorithm to estimate per-pixel convergence and stop sampling pixels once their estimated error falls below the threshold.

items.title: Russian Roulette
items.text: Terminates low-contribution paths while maintaining an unbiased estimator.

blocks.text: Four scheduling policies were implemented to compare static and runtime-aware workload organisation:

items.title: None
items.text: Preserves the original traversal order and provides the baseline.

items.title: Material
items.text: Groups shading records by material to improve shader and material-data locality.

items.title: Texture
items.text: Groups records according to texture access to target texture cache locality.

items.title: Cost-Benefit
items.text: Combines material grouping, spatial ordering and runtime shading-cost estimates to prioritise work according to expected contribution relative to execution cost.

blocks.text: The Cost-Benefit scheduler is the main research contribution. Runtime measurements are collected while rendering and used to estimate the cost of shading different materials and textures.

A per-material cost estimate is updated using an exponential moving average. The scheduler combines these estimates with accumulated ray throughput to calculate the expected contribution of shading work relative to its execution cost.

items.title: Runtime cost tracking
items.text: Measures shading cost during rendering and updates the estimates for subsequent scheduling passes.

items.title: Work prioritisation
items.text: Higher contribution relative to estimated cost receives higher scheduling priority.

items.title: Spatial ordering
items.text: Morton ordering is used within material groups to retain spatial locality.

items.title: Cost-aware termination
items.text: Russian Roulette incorporates estimated material cost into path termination decisions.

blocks.text: The scheduling policies were evaluated using two procedural OpenUSD benchmark scenes under identical rendering configurations. The Mixed Scene combines different geometry, materials and textures, while the Dragon Scene uses a higher triangle count with a more consistent distribution of geometry and materials.

items.title: Sample counts
items.text: 256, 1024, 2048 and 4096 samples per pixel.

items.title: Scheduling policies
items.text: None, Material, Texture and Cost-Benefit.

items.title: Measurements
items.text: Shading time, pipeline time, scheduling overhead, execution coherence, cache-line homogeneity and image difference.

items.title: Repetitions
items.text: Three independent runs were performed for each configuration.

blocks.text: Cost-Benefit produced the lowest shading time across both benchmark scenes and consistently improved on the unscheduled baseline. The improvement increased with rendering workload, reaching its largest reduction at the highest sample count.

items.title: 8–10% lower shading time at 4096 samples
items.text: At 4096 samples and 1080×1080 resolution, Cost-Benefit reduced shading time by 7.7% in the Mixed Scene and 9.6% in the Dragon Scene compared with the unscheduled baseline.

items.title: Improved execution coherence
items.text: At 4096 samples, Cost-Benefit produced average material run lengths of 1474.5 records in the Mixed Scene and 1560.7 in the Dragon Scene, compared with 2.9 and 2.8 for the baseline.

items.title: 98.9% material cache-line homogeneity
items.text: Cost-Benefit achieved material cache-line homogeneity of 98.9% in the Mixed Scene and 98.8% in the Dragon Scene, compared with 21.9% and 19.0% for the baseline.

items.title: Lowest total pipeline time
items.text: Cost-Benefit achieved the lowest total pipeline time across the evaluated experiments. The largest reduction occurred in shading, while smaller improvements were also observed in traversal. Scheduling introduced additional cost for runtime analysis, but this remained small relative to the time saved.

items.title: Minimal image differences
items.text: Comparison with the baseline produced mean luminance differences of 0.0088 in the Mixed Scene and 0.0100 in the Dragon Scene. Most differences were concentrated around the ceiling light and did not change the final rendered result.

blocks.text: The results show that execution coherence alone was not sufficient to obtain the best rendering performance. Material scheduling achieved similarly high coherence, but Cost-Benefit performed better by incorporating runtime execution cost into the scheduling decision.

This project was completed as my MSc research project in Computer Animation and Visual Effects at Bournemouth University, achieving a Distinction with a final grade of 87. The result reflects the substantial research, engineering and evaluation required to take the project from an initial research question through to a complete working renderer.

mocap.title: Motion Capture Retargeting & Cleanup
mocap.description: Unreal Engine 5 motion capture retargeting and cleanup pipeline using IK Rigs, IK Retargeter, Control Rig, and Houdini.

blocks.text: A motion capture retargeting and cleanup pipeline developed for the group project Eternally Dancing. The workflow uses Unreal Engine 5 to retarget AI-generated motion capture onto production characters, clean the animation using Control Rig, and refine the resulting motion in Houdini.

My contribution focused on investigating the motion capture workflow, defining the UE5 and Houdini pipeline, building the retargeting setup, and cleaning the resulting animations for use in the final project.

The project initially investigated several approaches for generating motion capture data. After testing multiple AI-based solutions against sample dance sequences, QuickMagic was selected for its ability to generate motion from recorded footage and refine tracking points before export.

items.title: Capture
items.text: Recorded dance footage following the requirements for the selected motion capture workflow.

items.title: AI Tracking
items.text: Generated animation from the recorded footage using QuickMagic.

items.title: 2D Refinement
items.text: Corrected tracking points before exporting the resulting animation.

blocks.text: The motion capture output was imported into Unreal Engine 5 and transferred onto the project's characters using the IK Rig and IK Retargeter systems. This allowed the captured performance to be adapted to different character skeletons while preserving the original movement.

items.title: IK Rig
items.text: Configured the source and target character skeletons with IK systems for pose adjustment and retargeting.

items.title: IK Retargeter
items.text: Mapped the captured animation onto the project's characters while maintaining the original performance.

items.title: Control Rig
items.text: Used Control Rig inside Unreal Engine Sequencer to manually refine poses and correct sections of the animation.

blocks.text: The retargeted animation was cleaned directly in Unreal Engine using Control Rig and Sequencer. Keyframes were added where required to correct the motion and refine larger body movements.

items.title: Ballet Animation
items.text: Refined the retargeted dance performance using Control Rig and Sequencer.

items.title: Stretch Animation
items.text: Applied the same cleanup workflow to a second animation used for the character transition.

items.title: Reference-driven Cleanup
items.text: Used the original performance as a reference when correcting poses and movement.

blocks.text: After the initial UE5 cleanup, the animations were transferred to Houdini for further procedural refinement. Houdini provided additional tools for inspecting and modifying the complete animation sequence.

items.title: MotionClip
items.text: Used MotionClip to inspect the complete animation sequence and edit motion procedurally.

items.title: Motion Processing
items.text: Used nodes such as Stabilize Joint and Smooth to refine the resulting animation.

items.title: Validation
items.text: Applied the cleaned animation to the project's 3D characters to verify the final result.

blocks.text: The final workflow separated the motion capture process into dedicated stages, using each application for the tasks it was best suited to handle.

items.title: Motion Capture
items.text: Recorded performance footage and generated the initial animation.

items.title: QuickMagic
items.text: Generated and refined the AI motion capture data.

items.title: Unreal Engine 5
items.text: Retargeted the animation using IK Rig and IK Retargeter, then performed manual cleanup with Control Rig.

items.title: Houdini
items.text: Performed additional procedural refinement and validation using animation processing nodes.

blocks.text: The project also involved supporting the wider production with procedural tools and technical fixes in Houdini.

items.title: VEX
items.text: Implemented VEX logic to dynamically control elements of the butterfly effects used around the character.

items.title: Butterfly Movement
items.text: Adjusted movement and normal orientation to prevent butterflies from behaving erratically around the dancer.

items.title: Transition Effects
items.text: Added controls to keep butterflies facing forward and maintain spacing during the transition spiral.

snowglobe.title: Real-Time Snow Globe Simulation
snowglobe.description: Real-time particle-based snow globe simulation using Position Based Dynamics, WebGL, and Three.js.

blocks.text: A real-time snow globe simulation developed to investigate particle-based techniques and Position Based Dynamics in a browser-based environment. The system combines Verlet integration, iterative constraints, spatial hashing, collision handling, and GPU instanced rendering to simulate thousands of particles interactively.

The simulation supports two particle behaviours: a marble mode designed around rigid particle collisions and a snow mode that produces more clustered and cohesive movement while maintaining stable real-time performance.
The simulation is structured as a sequence of particle update, neighbour search, constraint solving, collision handling, and rendering stages.

items.title: Integration
items.text: Verlet integration updates particle positions using current and previous positions.

items.title: Spatial Hashing
items.text: Particles are assigned to grid cells so neighbour searches only evaluate nearby particles.

items.title: Constraint Solver
items.text: Position Based Dynamics iteratively resolves particle overlaps and maintains minimum separation distances.

items.title: Collision Handling
items.text: Particles are constrained against the snow globe and simplified scene collision geometry.

items.title: Rendering
items.text: Three.js and WebGL render the particle system using GPU instancing.

blocks.text: The simulation uses Position Based Dynamics to maintain stable particle interactions by directly correcting particle positions rather than relying on traditional force-based integration. Multiple solver iterations are performed each frame to reduce overlap and improve collision stability.

items.title: Verlet Integration
items.text: Calculates particle movement from the difference between the current and previous positions.

items.title: Iterative Constraints
items.text: Repeatedly corrects particle positions to maintain separation and stable interactions.

items.title: Damping
items.text: Reduces excessive bouncing and helps particles settle after collisions.

blocks.text: Neighbour searches are accelerated using a spatial hashing grid. Instead of checking every particle against every other particle, each particle searches its current cell and the surrounding 26 cells.
This reduces the number of collision checks required as particle counts increase and was an important part of maintaining interactive performance with thousands of particles.
Two particle behaviours were implemented to explore different material responses within the same simulation framework.

items.title: Marble
items.text: Uses more rigid particle interactions, producing faster movement and more visible bouncing during collisions.

items.title: Snow
items.text: Reduces relative particle movement and encourages particles to settle together, producing a denser snow-like appearance.

blocks.text: The simulation runs entirely in the browser using TypeScript, WebGL, Three.js, and React Three Fiber. GPU instanced rendering allows thousands of particles to be drawn using a shared mesh and material, reducing the rendering overhead associated with individual particle draw calls.

items.title: GPU Instancing
items.text: Renders the particle system using instanced geometry to reduce draw calls.

items.title: Interactive Gravity
items.text: Rotating the snow globe changes the direction of gravity inside the simulation.

items.title: PBR Rendering
items.text: Uses physically based materials and HDR lighting for the final snow globe scenes.

blocks.text: Performance was evaluated by increasing the number of simulated particles and measuring the resulting average frame rate. The tests show how simulation and neighbour-search costs increase as particle density grows.

The simulation maintained interactive performance across the tested range, although performance decreased as particle counts increased. At higher densities, neighbour searches and collision solving became more expensive, making spatial hashing and GPU instanced rendering important for maintaining real-time interaction.

hair.title: Real-Time Hair Simulation & Rendering
hair.description: Real-time physically based hair simulation with CPU strand dynamics, GPU ribbon rendering, procedural follower strands, and interactive styling controls.

blocks.text: A real-time hair simulation and rendering system developed to explore physically based strand dynamics, GPU rendering techniques, procedural hair generation, collision handling, and interactive simulation controls.

The system combines CPU-side guide-strand simulation with GPU-side ribbon expansion and procedural follower strands, allowing visually dense hair to be rendered while keeping the physics workload manageable for real-time interaction.
The system separates hair generation, physical simulation, collision handling, GPU rendering, and user interaction into independent stages.

items.title: Scalp Sampling
items.text: Hair roots are generated from sampled regions of the character mesh using a distribution mask.

items.title: Strand Generation
items.text: Each guide strand is represented as a chain of particles connected by distance constraints.

items.title: Physics Simulation
items.text: Verlet integration and iterative positional constraints update strand motion while preserving segment lengths.

items.title: Collision Handling
items.text: Hair particles interact with ellipsoidal collision volumes fitted to the head and facial features.

items.title: GPU Upload
items.text: Simulated guide-strand segment data is streamed to the GPU using a Texture Buffer Object.

items.title: Ribbon Rendering
items.text: Guide segments are expanded into camera-facing ribbon geometry directly on the GPU.

items.title: Follower Generation
items.text: Additional strands are generated procedurally on the GPU to increase visual density without increasing CPU simulation cost.

blocks.text: Hair strands are represented as particle chains and simulated using Verlet integration. Instead of storing velocity explicitly, particle movement is reconstructed from current and previous positions, providing stable motion that integrates naturally with positional constraints.

items.title: Verlet Integration
items.text: Updates strand particles using positional history, acceleration, and damping.

items.title: Distance Constraints
items.text: Iterative positional corrections preserve the rest length between neighbouring particles.

items.title: Root Attachment
items.text: Root particles remain pinned to the animated head transform while the rest of the strand responds dynamically.

items.title: Wind
items.text: Directional wind and turbulence produce secondary motion with increasing influence towards the strand tips.

blocks.text: The system supports procedural hair styling while preserving the underlying physical simulation. Hair distribution is controlled using a grayscale scalp mask, allowing strands to be generated only within selected regions of the character mesh.

items.title: Straight Hair
items.text: Uses the simulated guide-strand structure directly for natural secondary motion.

items.title: Curly Hair
items.text: Uses a procedural sinusoidal rest-shape deformation with configurable amplitude, frequency, and per-strand phase.

items.title: Distribution Mask
items.text: Controls strand placement across the scalp to provide a natural hairline and artistic control over hair generation.

blocks.text: Hair collision is approximated using ellipsoidal volumes fitted to the character rather than more expensive mesh-level collision detection. Collision tests are performed in head-local space to simplify the calculations.

items.title: Head Collider
items.text: An ellipsoid approximates the overall head volume and prevents strands from penetrating the character.

items.title: Facial Colliders
items.text: Additional ellipsoids approximate the nose and mouth to improve interaction around facial features.

items.title: Surface Projection
items.text: Particles detected inside a collider are projected back onto its surface and friction is applied to reduce sliding artifacts.

blocks.text: The primary renderer avoids generating full cylindrical geometry for every strand. Instead, simulated guide-strand segments are uploaded to the GPU and expanded into camera-facing ribbon quads, reducing the amount of geometry required for dense hair.

items.title: Guide Strands
items.text: A reduced set of physically simulated strands provides the underlying hair motion.

items.title: Texture Buffer Objects
items.text: Guide-segment positions and radii are streamed to the GPU for rendering.

items.title: Ribbon Expansion
items.text: The vertex shader expands each guide segment into camera-facing ribbon geometry.

items.title: Follower Strands
items.text: Additional strands are generated procedurally on the GPU around each guide strand to create visually denser hair without simulating every strand individually.

blocks.text: Hair is rendered through a custom OpenGL 4.1 and GLSL pipeline with a simplified physically inspired shading model designed for thin directional geometry.

items.title: Hair Shading
items.text: Combines diffuse lighting, directional specular highlights, and rim lighting to approximate the anisotropic appearance of hair.

items.title: Alpha-to-Coverage
items.text: Uses multisampling and alpha-to-coverage to reduce transparency and aliasing artifacts across overlapping ribbons.

items.title: Dual Rendering
items.text: Supports both lightweight line rendering for debugging and GPU ribbon rendering for the final hair representation.

blocks.text: A PySide6 interface provides live control over the simulation and rendering system without requiring the application to restart or rebuild the scene.

items.title: Hair Controls
items.text: Adjust strand count, length, thickness, follower density, and hair style in real time.

items.title: Simulation Controls
items.text: Toggle wind and modify parameters affecting the physical behaviour of the strands.

items.title: Debugging
items.text: Visualise collision volumes and switch rendering modes while the simulation is running.

blocks.text: The rendering architecture is designed around simulating a limited number of guide strands on the CPU while generating additional visual density on the GPU. This keeps expensive physical simulation separate from the number of strands ultimately displayed.

items.title: Guide-Strand Simulation
items.text: Only the primary guide strands require full CPU physics simulation.

items.title: GPU Followers
items.text: Follower strands increase apparent hair density without introducing equivalent CPU simulation cost.

items.title: Adaptive Constraints
items.text: Constraint solving is structured to balance strand stability with simulation cost.

items.title: GPU Streaming
items.text: Texture Buffer Objects provide a compact path for transferring simulated strand data to the rendering pipeline.

rendermanApi.title: Procedural RenderMan Rendering
rendermanApi.description: Procedural modelling and rendering of a real-world salt shaker using Pixar RenderMan, Python, and Open Shading Language.

media.alt: RenderMan salt shaker model first reference
RenderMan salt shaker model second reference

blocks.text: A procedural rendering project exploring Pixar RenderMan's Python API through the recreation of a real household salt shaker from photographic reference.
The complete asset and scene were generated through code, combining procedural geometry, physically based materials, custom OSL shaders, HDR environment lighting, and camera effects.
The salt shaker was broken down into several independently generated components, allowing the geometry to be constructed and adjusted procedurally rather than through a traditional modelling package.

items.title: Glass Body
items.text: Generated from a profile curve and revolved around a central axis to create the rotationally symmetric container.

items.title: Inner Wall
items.text: Added to the main body to reproduce the thickness of the glass.

items.title: Neck and Support Ring
items.text: Constructed from cylindrical geometry and assembled separately from the main body.

items.title: Screw Thread
items.text: Generated procedurally around the neck to allow the cap and bottle to connect correctly.

items.title: Cap
items.text: Created as an independent procedural component so it could be positioned separately in the scene.

blocks.text: The scene is generated directly through RenderMan's Python API. The Python entry point creates the RenderMan context, configures the renderer, builds the scene, assigns lighting and materials, and exports the resulting RIB scene for rendering.

items.title: Scene Generation
items.text: Python constructs the complete RenderMan scene and exports the RIB representation.

items.title: Render Configuration
items.text: The renderer is configured with PxrPathTracer, ray-traced rendering, sampling controls, perspective projection, and depth of field.

items.title: Shader Compilation
items.text: Custom OSL shaders are compiled before scene generation and made available through the RenderMan shader search path.

items.title: Automated Rendering
items.text: A Makefile provides commands for scene generation, rendering, texture conversion, viewing, and cleaning generated files.

blocks.text: Different material responses were required for the frosted glass body, plastic cap, printed label, and wooden surface. RenderMan's PxrSurface shader was used as the primary BRDF model, with parameters tuned for each material.

items.title: Frosted Glass
items.text: Reflection, refraction, and roughness were balanced to reproduce the cloudy appearance of the reference object.

items.title: Plastic
items.text: The cap uses stronger diffuse response and softer specular highlights.

items.title: Custom OSL
items.text: Procedural shaders were developed for frosted glass and wood grain, introducing controlled surface variation.

items.title: Texture Mapping
items.text: The printed label and environmental surfaces use texture maps alongside procedural shading.

blocks.text: The lighting setup combines an HDR environment with manually positioned RenderMan lights. The HDR environment provides reflections and ambient illumination while additional lights reproduce the highlights and lighting direction visible in the reference photographs.

items.title: HDR Environment
items.text: A PxrDomeLight provides environment illumination and reflection information for the glass.

items.title: Key Light
items.text: A PxrSphereLight provides the primary directional lighting contribution.

items.title: Fill Light
items.text: A secondary warm light adds additional illumination and variation.

items.title: Highlight Lighting
items.text: Additional lights were positioned around the glass neck to control reflections and highlights.

blocks.text: Reference photographs were taken from multiple angles before modelling. The geometry, materials, camera and lighting were then iteratively adjusted against the photographs to reproduce the original composition.
Two final scenes were produced: one recreating the original reference composition and another presenting the completed salt shaker independently using the same lighting setup.

The final scene uses a perspective camera with RenderMan depth of field to reproduce subtle photographic characteristics from the reference images. The render uses PxrPathTracer with ray-traced rendering and increased sampling for the final image.

items.title: Perspective Camera
items.text: Configured to match the composition and viewing angle of the reference photographs.

items.title: Depth of Field
items.text: Applied subtly to soften areas outside the focal plane while preserving the overall composition.

items.title: Path Tracing
items.text: PxrPathTracer handles indirect lighting, reflections, refractions, and other ray-traced effects.

blocks.text: The project includes a small command-line rendering pipeline for automating the RenderMan workflow.

items.title: Texture Conversion
items.text: Source textures are converted into RenderMan's native texture format using txmake.

items.title: Scene Generation
items.text: The Python API generates the procedural geometry, shaders, camera, lights, and scene configuration.

items.title: RIB Export
items.text: The generated scene is exported as a RenderMan RIB file.

items.title: Rendering
items.text: The RIB scene is rendered using Pixar RenderMan and produces the final EXR output.

items.title: Review
items.text: Rendered output can be opened in the RenderMan framebuffer for inspection.

blocks.text: The final renders reproduced the main visual characteristics of the reference photographs, including the salt shaker's geometry, frosted glass, reflections, materials, lighting, and composition.
The project provided practical experience with procedural modelling, physically based shading, custom OSL development, HDR image-based lighting, and photorealistic rendering through RenderMan.

impossibleStairs.title: Impossible Stairs
impossibleStairs.description: Procedural staircase generation and ball animation system built with Python and PyMEL for Autodesk Maya.

media.alt: Procedurally generated impossible diamond stairs frontal view

blocks.text: A procedural Maya project exploring environment generation and character animation through Python and PyMEL.
The system generates impossible-style stair environments and drives a ball through them using procedural animation logic rather than manually keyframing each movement.
The environment is generated from reusable Python modules, allowing different architectural elements to be created and assembled directly inside Maya.

items.title: Stair Generation
items.text: Creates stepped geometry from configurable rise, run, depth, and step-count values, with a diagonal base supporting the staircase.

items.title: Torii Corridor
items.text: Duplicates and scales torii gates along a corridor while generating a progressively smaller staircase sequence behind them.

items.title: Radial Bricks
items.text: Generates wedge-shaped brick meshes and distributes them around a circular layout with configurable gaps.

blocks.text: The staircase is constructed procedurally from individual cubes. Each step is positioned using incremental horizontal run and vertical rise values, while a rotated base follows the diagonal direction of the stairs.

items.title: Step Creation
items.text: Individual step meshes are generated and positioned from the configured run and rise.

items.title: Base Generation
items.text: A diagonal base is calculated from the overall staircase dimensions and positioned beneath the steps.

items.title: Grouping
items.text: All generated geometry is placed under a common transform for easier scene management.

blocks.text: The ball animation system determines its bounce targets directly from the generated stair geometry. This allows the animation to adapt to the scene rather than relying on manually authored positions.

items.title: Target Collection
items.text: The system searches stair groups, identifies individual steps, and calculates the top-center position of each target using the ball radius.

items.title: Hop Timing
items.text: The available animation range is distributed across the required number of stair-to-stair hops.

items.title: Bounce Arc
items.text: Each hop is constructed from contact, squash, recovery, launch, impulse, apex, and landing phases.

items.title: Rolling
items.text: Ball rotation is accumulated from movement and velocity so the ball rolls naturally between contacts.

blocks.text: Squash and stretch are generated procedurally around each bounce to reinforce the impact and movement of the ball.

items.title: Contact
items.text: The ball compresses when reaching a stair surface.

items.title: Recovery
items.text: The ball returns to its upright form before launching into the next bounce.

items.title: Stretch
items.text: Vertical stretching is applied during the upward and pre-contact portions of the bounce.

items.title: Apex
items.text: The animation uses dedicated timing and tangent controls to produce smoother transitions around the peak.

blocks.text: The animation system supports both automatic stair traversal and explicitly defined step sequences, allowing different balls to follow different paths through the environment.

items.title: Automatic Traversal
items.text: The primary ball derives its targets from the configured stair-group order and step exclusions.

items.title: Custom Sequences
items.text: A secondary ball can be assigned an explicit sequence of stair groups and step numbers.

items.title: Animation Parameters
items.text: Jump power, squash amount, stretch amount, squash duration, impulse ratio, and total animation duration can be adjusted independently.

items.title: Curve Cleanup
items.text: Contact frames use linear tangents while apex frames receive weighted smooth tangents for more controlled motion.

blocks.text: The project is organised as a small procedural toolkit with separate modules for scene generation, animation, constants, and utility functions.

items.title: Environment
items.text: Python modules generate the staircase, torii corridor, and radial brick geometry.

items.title: Animation Setup
items.text: The animation system identifies the ball controls and derives the ball radius from its geometry.

items.title: Target Generation
items.text: Stair geometry is converted into a sequence of bounce targets.

items.title: Keyframe Generation
items.text: Procedural timing logic generates translation, rotation, and squash/stretch keyframes.

items.title: Scene Output
items.text: The resulting geometry and animation are created directly in Maya for further artistic adjustment.

blocks.text: The project produces reusable procedural environment modules and an animation system capable of driving a ball through generated stair layouts without manually defining every bounce.

The resulting toolkit combines procedural modelling with animation automation, providing a foundation for generating variations of the environment and adapting the animation to different stair configurations.

hdaGarden.title: Garden Generator
hdaGarden.description: Procedural Japanese garden generation HDA for Houdini with interactive painting, terrain tools, and configurable environment systems.

blocks.text: A Houdini Digital Asset for procedurally generating Japanese-style gardens with configurable terrain, vegetation, paths, rocks, fences, rivers, and bridges.

The HDA combines procedural environment generation with interactive viewport tools, allowing artists to generate a garden layout, paint geometry placement, edit curves, and switch between simplified and production-level assets.
The generator supports multiple garden layouts through a single HDA, with different systems becoming available depending on the selected garden type.

items.title: Zen
items.text: Generates rock arrangements and procedural sand patterns with options including combined, rings, lines, sunburst, and checker patterns.

items.title: Tea
items.text: Generates structured walking paths using configurable rock styles, spacing, scale variation, and an editable path curve.

items.title: Strolling
items.text: Generates flowing river layouts with optional bridge geometry and an editable river path.

items.title: Custom
items.text: Uses a user-provided garden layout map to define a custom terrain pattern.

blocks.text: Terrain generation is controlled through garden dimensions, layout configuration, custom UV mapping, and surface bump parameters.

items.title: Garden Dimensions
items.text: Controls the overall width and depth of the generated garden.

items.title: Layout Maps
items.text: Predefined maps are used for Zen and Tea layouts, while Custom mode accepts a user-defined garden layout map.

items.title: Surface Detail
items.text: Non-strolling gardens use configurable noise-based bump settings to introduce terrain variation.

items.title: Strolling Terrain
items.text: Uses separate lacunarity, roughness, element size, and amplitude controls for the floor surface.

blocks.text: Garden elements can be enabled independently and procedurally distributed across the generated terrain. Density, scale variation, rotation, colour, and random seeds provide control over the final environment.

items.title: Bamboo
items.text: Can be painted interactively onto the terrain with configurable height and size variation.

items.title: Plants
items.text: Supports three independently configurable plant layers with density, iterations, scale variation, randomisation, and colour controls.

items.title: Grass
items.text: Generates surface vegetation with configurable length, thickness, and colour.

items.title: Pebbles
items.text: Distributes pebbles across the terrain with configurable scale, placement density, rotation, and colour.

items.title: Fences
items.text: Generates boundaries from an interactively editable curve with configurable height, resolution, and colour.

blocks.text: The HDA provides interactive viewport tools for painting vegetation and editing garden curves directly on the generated environment.

items.title: Geometry Painting
items.text: Artists can paint bamboo and three plant types directly onto the terrain.

items.title: Fence Editing
items.text: Fence geometry can be shaped interactively using an editable viewport curve.

items.title: Rock Path Editing
items.text: Tea garden paths can be created and adjusted through an interactive curve.

items.title: River Editing
items.text: The Strolling garden river can be shaped interactively before previewing its simulation.

blocks.text: The HDA uses a custom Python interaction layer to control Houdini's Scene Viewer and expose internal paint and curve tools directly through the asset interface. Rather than requiring artists to manually navigate into the HDA and activate individual nodes, Python switches the Scene Viewer to the appropriate internal node state and returns the user to the parent asset when the tool is exited.

The implementation uses Houdini's event loop callbacks to monitor the active viewer state and detect when the artist exits the internal tool. Active watchers are stored in hou.session, allowing multiple HDA instances and tool states to be tracked independently while preventing duplicate callbacks.

items.title: Tool State Entry
items.text: Dedicated Python functions launch the bamboo, plant, fence, rock path, and river editing tools by locating the corresponding internal node and entering its current Houdini viewer state.

items.title: Scene Viewer Control
items.text: The Scene Viewer is redirected to the internal tool node before entering its interactive state, allowing the artist to work directly in the viewport without leaving the HDA workflow.

items.title: Event Loop Monitoring
items.text: A hou.ui event loop callback continuously monitors the Scene Viewer state and detects when the active tool has been exited.

items.title: Context-Aware Exit
items.text: The system distinguishes between normal viewport navigation and an actual tool exit, preventing accidental context switches while the artist is working.

items.title: Automatic HDA Return
items.text: When an exit is detected, the Scene Viewer is returned to the parent HDA and the viewer is placed back into the Select state.

items.title: Watcher Management
items.text: Callbacks are registered using a unique HDA and tool key, allowing existing watchers to be removed before a new one is installed and preventing duplicate event-loop callbacks.

blocks.text: The HDA supports replacing simplified proxy geometry with higher-quality production assets for final scene output.

items.title: Proxy Workflow
items.text: Dummy geometry provides lightweight assets for viewport blocking and interactive painting.

items.title: Production Assets
items.text: Grass, pebbles, bamboo, three plant types, and Zen rocks can use higher-resolution external geometry.

items.title: Performance
items.text: Artists can work with simplified geometry during layout and switch to detailed assets when reviewing the final result.

blocks.text: Zen mode focuses on minimal garden compositions using procedural rock placement and raked sand patterns.

items.title: Rock Placement
items.text: Rock position, height, scale variation, randomisation, and colour can be controlled procedurally.

items.title: Sand Patterns
items.text: Five pattern styles are available: Combined, Rings, Lines, Sunburst, and Checkers.

items.title: Pattern Controls
items.text: Spacing, strength, ring limits, ray counts, and checker scale control the resulting sand deformation.

blocks.text: Tea mode generates a structured walking path using procedurally arranged stepping stones.

items.title: Rock Path
items.text: A configurable sequence of stepping stones is distributed along an editable path curve.

items.title: Rock Style
items.text: The path supports both circular and square stone styles.

items.title: Variation
items.text: Rock amount, separation, scale range, and colour can be adjusted to change the appearance of the path.

blocks.text: Strolling mode introduces a flowing river system and optional bridge geometry to create a navigable garden layout.

items.title: River Path
items.text: The river layout is controlled through an editable curve with configurable resolution and radius.

items.title: Variable Width
items.text: Independent scale controls at the beginning and end of the river allow the path to taper or widen.

items.title: Bridge
items.text: An external bridge geometry asset can be positioned, rotated, and scaled along the river.

items.title: FLIP Simulation
items.text: The river node contains a FLIP Solver that can be previewed to inspect the river animation.

blocks.text: The HDA is designed as a self-contained production tool with project-relative asset paths, interactive viewport workflows, procedural generation, and replaceable external geometry.

items.title: Project Setup
items.text: A base directory defines the root project path used to resolve maps, textures, geometry, and other external assets.

items.title: Garden Configuration
items.text: Artists select the garden dimensions and layout type before configuring the corresponding environment systems.

items.title: Interactive Layout
items.text: Geometry and curves can be painted or edited directly in the viewport.

items.title: Procedural Generation
items.text: The HDA generates the selected terrain and environment elements from the configured parameters.

items.title: Production Assets
items.text: Proxy geometry can be replaced with higher-resolution external assets for final rendering.

blocks.text: The Garden Generator provides a reusable Houdini asset for creating multiple Japanese-style garden environments from a single procedural tool.

The combination of procedural generation, interactive viewport tools, configurable layouts, and production-geometry support allows the same HDA to be used for both environment exploration and higher-quality scene output.
